<meta>This page features a parchment fragment from a Hebrew manuscript that was later repurposed as a book cover. This practice, known as "maculature," was common when parchment was a valuable commodity and older or "obsolete" manuscripts were cut up to reinforce newer bindings. The text here is a liturgical poem (piyyut), likely intended for a prayer service or festival. Due to the way the parchment was trimmed and folded for the binding, much of the text is cut off at the margins.</meta>

## The Eighth Experiment / Concerning the Salt Just Mentioned.

Take one part of the aforementioned **animated spirit** <term>Animated spirit: a substance "brought to life" or activated through specific alchemical processes, usually involving multiple distillations to concentrate its essence</term> and three parts of perfectly **rectified** <term>Rectified: purified through repeated distillation to achieve the highest possible purity and potency</term> ***water of life*** <note>original: *Aqua vitæ* — typically referring to highly concentrated ethanol or a potent alchemical solvent</note>, and pour it over such animated spirit. ## The Tenth Experiment

Take the same putrefied urine <note>in early modern chemistry, urine was a primary source for discovering phosphorus and ammonia</note> and place it into a vessel that has a high neck. Stop the opening with cotton tied to a hempen thread so that, whenever necessary, you may pull it out. This stopper should be soaked in oil, yet squeezed out again. Place an <term>Alembic</term> <note>the lid or "head" of a distilling apparatus, which catches rising vapors and directs them into a cooling tube</note> upon the vessel with well-sealed joints. First, apply the lowest heat, then increase it until it **sublimates** <note>the process where a substance is heated into a vapor and then collects as a solid on the cooler parts of the apparatus</note>. This is the **sublimated salt** that we have used, though we extracted only a small amount of it because the matter was not well sublimated beforehand and is only separated from its <term>Phlegm</term> <note>original: *Phlegmate* — the watery, inactive, or "tasteless" component left over or distilled during a chemical process</note> with great difficulty. 

At first, we marveled at this experiment; however, once we recognized the cause of its behavior, it did not seem as potent to us as other salts were, and therefore we let it go <note>the author implies they abandoned this specific method in favor of more effective alchemical salts</note>.

## The Tenth Experiment.

Take that same **putrefied urine** <note>urine allowed to sit and decompose, which alchemists used as a source of ammonia</note> and place it in a vessel that has a high neck. Plug it with cotton that is tied to a hempen thread, so that you may pull it out whenever necessary. This stopper should be soaked in oil and then squeezed out again. Place an **alembic** <note>the peaked cap of a distilling apparatus that directs vapors into a cooling tube</note> upon the vessel, ensuring the joints are well-secured.

At first, provide the lowest possible heat; thereafter, increase it until the substance **sublimates** <note>original: *sublimiert*. The process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then cools back into a solid form, effectively purifying it</note>. This is the **sublimated salt** that we have used, though we extracted very little of it because the material had not been well sublimated beforehand and is separated from its **phlegm** <note>original: *Phlegmate*. In alchemy, this refers to the watery, tasteless, and chemically inactive byproduct of distillation</note> only with great difficulty.

Initially, we were surprised by this experiment, but once we recognized the underlying cause, we did not consider it as potent as other salts were; for that reason, we have set it aside.

# The Eleventh Experiment, concerning Human Blood.

Take blood drawn from healthy and **choleric** <note>original: *Colerischen*. In the medieval theory of the four humors, a "choleric" person was characterized as hot and dry, which alchemists believed influenced the chemical properties of their blood</note> men; lay it upon a clean tablet to dry, so that the **phlegm** <note>original: *Phlegma*. A term used in alchemy to describe the watery, tasteless, and chemically inactive part of a substance</note> may be separated from it.

Once it is well dried, grind it thoroughly and place it into a glass vessel. Distill a "water" from it with gentle heat; keep this water separate. Thereafter, set the receiver back in place and increase your heat a little, but not too much, so that the **salt** does not **sublimate** <note>original: *sublimire*. The process where a substance turns from a solid into a gas and then back into a solid form, used here as a method of purification</note> and only the remaining moisture and the **oil** pass over. Continue this process until nothing more will pass over.

Then, let the vessel cool and take the **burnt earth** <note>the solid, charred residue or "caput mortuum" left behind after all liquids have been driven off</note> and put it into a separate vessel. Seal it well so that nothing escapes; for if it were exposed to air, the contents of the vessel, along with the material or earth, would dissipate. Place it in a <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>original: *Reuerber*. A furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" heat from the roof onto the material, allowing for intense heat without direct contact with the fuel</note> and

Strain the <term>solution <note>The liquid resulting from the dissolution of mercury in the mineral mercurial water described on the previous page.</note></term> carefully, so that if any earthy <term>matter</term> should remain at the bottom, it may be separated from this <term>solution</term>; for it would not be good for the <term>feces <note>original: Feces; in alchemy, this refers to the solid dregs, dross, or impurities that settle at the bottom of a vessel.</note></term> to be carried over. Afterward, take the aforementioned <term>mercury</term> that has been <term>dissolved</term> and <term>putrefy <note>Putrefaction is the process of subjecting a substance to gentle, consistent heat over a long period to break it down and prepare it for transformation.</note></term> it for 30 days in a <term>water bath <note>original: Balneo; referring to a Balneum Mariae or Bain-Marie, which provides indirect, steady heat.</note></term> or in warm manure, which must always be changed every ten days so that the heat remains constant and is not extinguished. ### Experiments <note>original: "Experimenta."</note>

Close the vessel well with its **blind helm** <note>A still-head without a spout, used to seal a vessel during digestion so that vapors condense and fall back down rather than being collected.</note>; place it in a **balneum** <term>balneum</term> <note>A water bath (bain-marie) used for gentle, steady heating.</note> for 24 hours. Afterward, remove the blind helm; place before it a **receiver** <note>A vessel designed to collect the distilled liquid.</note> with an attached **alembic** <note>A distillation cap with a downward-pointing beak.</note>, well sealed, and distill the water over the ashes <note>An ash-bath, which provides a higher, dryer heat than a water bath.</note> with gentle fire. When you then see that the water has completely passed over at that degree of fire, remove the receiver with the water, seal and preserve it well. Place another [receiver], also well secured, in its place, and increase the fire so that the **air** <note>original: "Lufft"; in this context, it refers to the gaseous spirits or the most volatile vapors of the substance.</note> passes over entirely by itself. Once that has passed over, let the vessel cool and pour back over the **earth** <note>original: "erden"; the solid residue or "feces" remaining at the bottom of the distillation vessel.</note> as much of the distilled water as is needed to rise four fingers high above it. Place a blind helm upon it, well secured; set it in the water bath for 2 hours. Then remove the blind helm, place an alembic upon it and a receiver before it, all well secured, and distill it over with gentle fire on the ashes.

# Experiments

# Preface

...informed, you should first highly exercise yourself in **Theory** or **Speculation** <term>Speculation: In this context, the deep intellectual contemplation of natural laws and the structure of matter.</term>, as well as in **Practice**, and test your opinion with certain reasons or *rationales* <note>original: "Rationibus"</note>, as well as with true experience.

...then, which paths you should have perceived, so blame your own lack of understanding and stubbornness for this, and do not hold other people in contempt, since they gave you no cause for such contempt. This little book, however, which will follow, I divide into four parts.

In the first part, I will speak of the discovery of this **Art** <term>Art</term> <note>The "Great Art" (Ars Magna) of alchemy, specifically the quest for the Philosopher's Stone.</note> and of the wise men who likewise, as I have, possessed it and truly knew it. <meta>catchword: would</meta>

If none were separated from the others in their **generation** <note>original: *Generation*. In this context, it refers to the process by which a substance is born or created in nature.</note>, each could become the other, which is quite **absurd** <note>original: *absurdum*</note> to hear. Through this, it also clearly appears that the four **elements** <note>original: *Elementa*</note> remain as they are and are not the **first matter of metals** <note>original: *materia metallorum*</note>.

Furthermore, if it were true that the **elements** were the **primary matter of metals** <note>original: *prima materia metallorum*</note>, it would follow that one could make humans and other things out of metals; for humans are also made from the four elements. From this, it would then arise that everything was merely assigned by chance, and there would be no **distinction** in **Nature**. Instead, when Nature intended to **produce** <note>original: *producieren*</note> a tree, an animal could just as easily come from it, and the **philosophical maxim** <note>original: *Philosophische Spruch*</note> would come to nothing, where they say: **Everything that generates naturally produces its own likeness** <note>original Latin: *Omne generans naturaliter generat suum simile*</note>. For then each thing would not be able to generate its own kind, and it would depend on luck what might yet become of it.

# Part Four

# S A Y I N G S
<note>original: *DICTA*</note>

Of the **Body** <note>original: *Corporis*</note>, seal it up, set it in the ashes, and let it cook thus for three months. In this way, that which is hidden—that is, the **Soul** <note>original: *Anima*</note>—becomes manifest; and that which is manifest—that is, **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note>—becomes hidden.

# Of the Great Stone

The constant **Salt** <note>original: "Saltz." # The Tenth Key.

In our **Stone** <note>The Philosopher’s Stone, the legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note>—made by me and long before me—are contained all the **Elements**, all mineral and metallic forms, and indeed all the qualities and properties of the entire world. For within it must be found the greatest and most powerful **heat**; because through its great internal **fire**, the cold body of **Saturn** <note>original: *Saturni*; the alchemical name for the metal lead.</note> is warmed and, through such ignition, is transformed into the very best **gold**. There must also be found within it the greatest **cold**, because through its addition, the heated degree of **Venus** <note>original: *Veneris*; the alchemical name for the metal copper.</note> is tempered, and the living **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*; quicksilver, which alchemists sought to "fix" or solidify.</note> is **coagulated** <note>Solidified or brought from a liquid/vaporous state into a stable, solid form.</note>; and in the same way, through its solidification, it must become good, enduring gold. The reason for this is that all such properties have been poured into the **matter** <note>original: *materia*; the raw substance used to begin the alchemical Great Work.</note> of our Great Stone by **Nature**. These properties must be boiled out and ripened through the **degrees of fire** <note>original: *Gradus ignis*; the controlled stages of increasing heat used in a furnace to mature the chemical mixture.</note>.

and the Stone have become a pure and singular <term>Medicine</term><note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" refers to the final, perfected state of the Philosophers' Stone, which can "heal" base metals into gold or the human body into health.</note>, of a quite subtle, spiritual, and penetrating property. For without the ferment of gold, the Stone cannot work well or produce its <term>Tincture</term>, because it is too subtle and penetrating. However, if it is fermented and combined with its like <note>Meaning, the Stone is joined with physical gold to give it "body."</note>, then the prepared Tincture attains an entrance or <term>Ingress</term><note>original: "Ingreß" — from the Latin ingressus, meaning the power of the substance to enter into and permeate a base metal.</note> to work upon other things. Take then one part of the prepared <term>Ferment</term><note>The fermented Stone that has been merged with gold.</note> for every thousand parts of the molten metals that you wish to <term>tinge</term><note>original: "tingieren" — the alchemical act of transforming a substance's nature and color, usually into gold.</note>. Know then, in the highest truth and word of all the world, that all such metal must become good, stable gold. For one body then gladly grasps another body; even if it is not its equal, it must nevertheless be forcefully brought to become its like through power and might, since like is born from like.

Whoever uses this means, to him all constancy and stability shall be revealed.

# ON THE FIRST MAT-
# TER OF THE PHILO-
### S O P H E R S' STONE.
<note>original Latin: "DE PRIMA MATERIA LAPIDIS PHILOSOPHICI." The "First Matter" is the raw, base substance that alchemists believed could be purified and transformed into the Stone.</note>

**A** stone is found, it is not dear,
From it a volatile <term>fire</term><note>original: "flüchtig fewr" — In alchemy, "volatile" refers to a substance that easily vaporizes or escapes the fire, often associated with the spirit or Mercury.</note> is drawn clear.
Of which the stone itself is wrought,
From White and Red together brought.
It is a stone, and yet no stone,
In it nature works alone.
From it there springs a fountain clear,
That drowns its fixed Father <note>The "fixed Father" usually represents Sulfur or the solid, stable aspect of the matter that must be dissolved.</note> here.
Devouring him with life and limb,
Until the soul returns to him.
And his volatile Mother has become
His equal in his kingdom's home.
He indeed in strength and might,
Has attained a much greater height.
The Son in maturity <note>original: "Alter" (age)</note> now excels,
His flying Mother he has prepared well.
Through <term>Vulcan</term><note>The Roman god of fire; here representing the alchemist's furnace or the controlled heat of the chemical process.</note> as it was before,
The Father through the Spirit born once more.
Body, Soul, and Spirit in two reside,
From which the whole work does subside.
From one source only does it spring,
And binds the volatile and fixed thing.
